Foil · broadcast video · pose + scoreboard

Fence
Vision

Six-class action recognition for foil fencing, from ordinary broadcast video. No sensors, no instrumented equipment, no marked piste.

Two fencers are located and tracked, 33 pose landmarks are extracted from each, and an LSTM classifies what both are doing twenty times a second. A second pipeline reads the broadcast scoreboard to recover when touches landed and who scored, with no OCR.

Action recognition

73.6% on six classes, and it travels

The classifier reads advance, retreat, lunge, parry, walking and neutral for each fencer independently, against a majority-class baseline of 34.8%. Every figure below comes from a bout the model never trained on.

It survives a venue change

Two bouts were held out at venues the model had never seen — different hall, lighting, camera, broadcaster — and scored 73.7% and 69.1%, four to six points below a familiar bout. Roughly a minute of labelled footage from a new venue closes most of that gap, which makes deployment a small known cost rather than a research problem.

Left-handers were a blind spot

Pose normalisation removes translation and scale but not handedness. The training corpus happened to hold only one handedness in its right-hand slot, and a left-handed fencer at a new venue scored 35% while their opponent scored 71%. Mirroring the sequences fixed it and helped generally, worth 7 points against a matched control.

Each fencer sees the other

A retreat means something different when the opponent is lunging, so every fencer's feature vector carries their opponent's alongside their own. Reducing the sequence with its last state rather than a mean is worth another 4 to 5 points: a parry lasts about 0.6 s inside a 2 s window, and averaging buries it.

Parry needed a better shape, not better numbers

Parry is brief, small, and overlaps with footwork — the raw classifier ran at 29% precision. Replacing two independent thresholds with a single fitted line, letting strong parry evidence trade against a committed attack, took F1 from 0.31 to 0.38 with overall accuracy unchanged. Re-tuning the old thresholds gained nothing, so it was the shape of the rule that mattered.

Scoreboard

Reading the graphics without OCR

Broadcast overlays sit at fixed positions, so comparing digit images beats recognising characters. Scores only ever rise, which turns reading them into a constrained search. The reader recovers halt times, which lamps fired, and who scored.

Fifty-four percent of touches are single-lamp, where the lamp alone names the scorer. Hand labelling drops to the contested remainder — 40% of the work.

Research question

Can it tell who had right of way?

When both lamps fire, the referee awards the touch on right of way: priority goes to whoever attacked first. This is the part of fencing a scoreboard cannot settle, so it is the only place an action model can contribute.

A fencer labelled every contested halt by the kind of action it was, from video alone, before seeing any model output. The four categories were fixed in advance, each with its own prediction about what the model should do.

On clean attacks it reaches 0.84 — two fifths of all contested halts, and the model recovers the referee's call on them. What makes the rest interesting is that each category fails for a reason that was predicted in advance.

close-blade

Close quarters, a fast series of blade actions. A human follows it; the tracker cannot. The signal stays full-size and points the wrong way as often as the right way — a perception limit.

both attack

Both go forward and the call turns on a fine margin. Because both advance, the difference the model measures cancels toward zero — its magnitude falls to 0.65 against 0.99 for clean attacks, exactly as registered before these labels existed.

attack in prep

Priority goes to the fencer moving back, who lunges into the other’s preparation. The rule inverts the measurement: the fencer going forward is the one without priority. Registered prediction was "below chance", and this is the lowest figure in the project.

What the pooled number does and does not support. Across all 104 contested halts the model ranks the referee's call at 0.61 AUC (95% CI [0.50, 0.72], p = 0.026). That clears significance alone but not after correcting for the three pre-registered features, and the attack-in-prep figure rests on seven halts. The category breakdown is the result worth quoting; the single average is not.

Method

Built to be wrong in public

Pre-registered, then tested

The right-of-way feature was chosen on two bouts and then frozen. Every later bout was a held-out test, with the statistic, direction and subgroup written down before the data existed. A rival hypothesis of my own — that priority could be recovered from who moved first — was registered three times and failed all three.

The instrument has a resolution

That rival hypothesis failed for a measurable reason. The action signal smooths over 1.25–1.58 s, and foil's lockout is 0.30 s. Timing an onset that fine is five times beyond what the instrument resolves, and would be with a perfect classifier.

The right-of-way estimate as held-out data arrived. The last step was not new data: two video files turned out to be the same match, and removing the duplicate moved the number again.
